newsitem.title: UK: Major's aides cool British election fever.
newsitem.headline: Major's aides cool British election fever.

text.p: Officials from British Prime Minister John Major's office cooled speculation that a Thursday cabinet meeting might be followed by the announcement of an election.
"I'm not expecting a press conference," one aide said.
He said he did not expect the cabinet meeting, which began at 1030 GMT, to hold a political discussion after regular government business.
Most politicians expect the election to take place on May 1, leaving Major just seven weeks to rescue the dismal fortunes of his struggling party.
But they disagree over whether the Conservatives' interests would be best served by an extended election campaign launched by Major this week or a short, concentrated one.
If the date were announced this week, Major could use a speech he is due to deliver on Saturday to the annual meeting of his party's Central Council to launch his campaign.
The aide declined to hint when an election might be held, saying: "I'm not going to rule out an election statement. When an election statement is to be made...I will tell you."

The opposition Labour Party is some 20 points ahead in opinion polls. On Wednesday leader Tony Blair warned supporters against complacency, saying: "Though many people may write off the Tories, and take the voters' verdict for granted, I for one do not."

Most Cabinet ministers going into the meeting declined to answer questions. Finance Minister Kenneth Clarke smiled and told reporters: "No news for any of you". Major is constitutionally required to hold an election by May 22, but April 17 is now seen as the only realistic alternative to May 1.
Before announcing any date, Major would have to ask Queen Elizabeth to approve arrangements for polling.
Major's aides shrugged off questions about a meeting between the two on Thursday, saying the prime minister had a routine meeting with the queen on Tuesday.
In recent days, the Conservatives have unveiled a raft of policies designed to convince voters that they have not run out of steam and deserve a fifth successive election victory.

Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell on Wednesday announced plans for a new law to virtually end the role of local councils in running homes for the elderly, leaving the job to commercial organisations and voluntary bodies.
Other recent initiatives have included a plan to reduce the state's role in pension provision by letting workers use tax breaks to purchase provision for their old age.
But Conservative efforts to revive their fortunes have been hindered by a spate of damaging controversies.

Allegations that a failure to enforce inspection standards at abattoirs is putting meat-eating Britons at risk of exposure to lethal bacteria forced Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg to make a statement to parliament on Wednesday.

The ruling party was also hit by a report on Thursday that parliament's Conservative-dominated Education and Employment Committee had slammed a new government initiative for a voucher system for nursery schooling.
The upsets appeared to leave the political initiative with Labour, which under Blair has shed many of its traditional socialist policies and moved to the political centre.
